question: What is the main goal of a therapeutic nurse-patient relationship?

options.A: Sharing personal stories with the client
options.B: The health and recovery of the patient

explanation: Spot on! Unlike friendships where both people share personal matters, a nurse-patient relationship is all about helping the patient heal and get better. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why do patients feel comfortable sharing their private health stories with nurses?

options.A: Because hospital regulations force them to speak
options.B: To test the clinical knowledge of the student
options.C: To pass the time during hospital visiting hours
options.D: Because they feel safe and trust the nurse

explanation: You got it! When patients know you genuinely care and won't judge them, they feel safe enough to open up about sensitive health issues. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h1)

question: During which phase of the nurse-patient relationship do you first meet and start building trust?
explanation: Correct! The orientation phase is your opening move—it's when you introduce yourself, break the ice, and let the patient know they are in good hands. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h2)

question: A patient is being discharged from the surgical ward today. Which relationship phase are you in?
explanation: Well done! Saying goodbye as a patient goes home or transfers to another ward marks the termination phase, wrapping up your care journey together. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which type of question encourages a patient to talk openly about how they are feeling?
explanation: Exactly! Asking questions like 'How have you been feeling today?' gives patients space to share their story in their own words. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h3)

question: What happens when your words say one thing, but your body language shows something completely different?

options.A: It has no impact on the patient experience
options.B: It speeds up the clinical recovery process
options.C: It destroys trust and causes confusion
options.D: It reassures the client more effectively

explanation: Spot on! Patients read our body language just as much as our words. Mixed signals make us look untrustworthy. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h3)

question: Telling an anxious patient 'Don't worry, everything will be fine' is an example of what communication mistake?
explanation: Correct! While we mean well, empty promises brush off the patient's real fears and shut down honest conversation. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h4)

question: Which of these is actually a helpful communication skill, NOT a barrier?
explanation: You nailed it! Active listening builds a strong bridge with your patient, while defensiveness, stereotyping, and rushing to give advice all block good care. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is it called when a nurse accidentally projects personal feelings or baggage onto a patient?
explanation: Spot on! Countertransference happens when our own personal emotions spill over and cloud how we treat a client. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why do nurses need to maintain strict professional boundaries with patients?

options.A: To encourage nurses to form romantic bonds with clients
options.B: To eliminate the need for documenting care plans
options.C: To make sure nurses do not talk to patients at all
options.D: To protect objectivity and ensure safe patient care

explanation: Correct! Boundaries keep your head clear so you can make sound, professional clinical decisions without emotional clutter. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is the biggest danger of poor communication among members of the healthcare team?

options.D: Slower internet speed on the ward

explanation: You got it! When nurses, doctors, and pharmacists fail to talk clearly, important details slip through the cracks, which can harm the patient. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h6)

question: You notice a doctor wrote a drug dose that looks unsafe for a patient. What should you do?

options.A: Speak up assertively to clarify the order before giving the drug
options.B: Complain to the patient about the incompetence of the medical team
options.C: Throw away the prescription chart and ignore the drug entirely
options.D: Administer the medication anyway to avoid arguing with the doctor

explanation: Spot on! Patient safety comes first. Always speak up respectfully and check with the prescriber if a medication order doesn't look right. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is a great way for a nurse to check their own personal biases and emotional triggers?
explanation: Correct! Taking time to pause and reflect on your own thoughts helps you catch hidden biases before they affect your patient care. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why do nursing students benefit from keeping a reflective journal after their clinical shifts?

options.A: It replaces the need for hospital incident reporting books
options.B: It helps them analyze and improve their relational skills
options.C: It stops patients from asking too many questions
options.D: It guarantees a higher score on written board exams

explanation: You nailed it! Writing down what went well (and what didn't) after a shift is one of the best ways to grow into a confident, caring nurse. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T1#GNS112_U3_T1_h7)
